form: nɬeʔkepmxcín ( a.k.a. Thompson River Salish ; ISO 639 -3: thp) is a Northern Interior Salish language spoken along the Fraser , Thompson, Nicola, and Coldwater rivers in British Columbia, Canada. The language has several dialects, including ƛ̓q̓əmcín (Lytton) and scw̕exmxcín (Nicola Valley). Bev Phillips is a first language speaker of nɬeʔkepmxcín from Lytton. According to Gessner, Herber, & Parker (2022), the language had approximately 105 fluent speakers at that time. There are active community efforts towards language retention and revitalization. To date , there has been only a single book of glossed nɬeʔkepmxcín speech that has been published (Egesdal, Thompson, & Jimmie, 2011 ). There have also been glossed stories and conversations published individually. See, for example, Koch (2011); Hannon, Stacey, & Steiner (2023); Hall & Phillips (2024, 2025); and Garcia, Hannan, & Stacey. (2025).

form: On October 23, 2025, Bev told the story to members of UBC’s nɬeʔkepmxcín Lab (nɬab) over the online meeting application Zoom . Alongside the Zoom recording, we recorded loss -less, uncompressed audio using the online application Fieldwork DRAWL ( Ducharme 2021, Lo & Ducharme 2021).1 This recording is published in tandem with the paper , so readers may listen along. After the October 2025 recording, she shared with us her original version of story which was written using the orthography commonly used in Lytton. Using the written version, Bev indicated the beginning and end of each sentence and volunteered a translation for each one. From there, the other authors transcribed the story using the North American Phonetic Alphabet (NAPA) as employed by Thompson & Thompson in their grammar (1992) and their dictionary (1996).2 We use this orthography instead of the Lytton one because this is the orthography used in the dictionary, which is used by many community me mbers, and in the linguistic literature on the language. The authors then glossed each sentence.

who: Bev Phillips, Brent Hall, Lisa Matthewson and Danica Reid
form: For the transcription, since the only standard for spelling and stress marking is the dictionary, we have tried to stay as close as possible to the spelling and stress marking in the dictionary, only deviating when needed to accurately represent Bev’s pronunciation. To our knowledge, there is no standardized system of separating words with spaces in the language, so we have come up with a pattern that largely mirrors Bev’s usage of spaces in her writing. For the most part, this means we use spaces the same way as Thompson & Thompson (1992, 1996) with the primary difference being that we treat certain contractions and clusters of proclitics as separate words. To our knowledge there is no standardized system of pun ctuation for the language, and some speakers prefer English punctuation not to be used , so we omit it entirely. Instead of separating sentences with periods, we separate them by beginning each sentence on a new line. This section also contains timestamps corresponding to the beginning of each new sentence in the accompanying audio file. In the interlinear gloss section, we use a four-line presentation.3 The four lines of our interlinear gloss, from top to bottom, are the orthography or transcription line, the segmentation line, the gloss line, and the translation line. The orthography line contains the transcription of each sentence using the NAPA based orthography from Thompson & Thompson (1992, 1996). This orthography roughly corresponds to surface representations of each morpheme. For example, deleted sounds are not present while inserted sounds are . In the segmentation line , each morpheme is written in its underlying representation. The next line is the gloss line which provides the correspondence between morphemes and their meanings. The translation line provides the English translation as volunteered by Bev.

form: Bev was ins pired to write this story from working with members of the nɬeʔekpmxcín lab. This work has included sharing stories, having conversations with other speakers, and taking part in targeted linguistic elicitations. Having worked with the lab for nearly four years now, she is able to take elicitation material that has been prepared for her and recognize who created it. She makes these judgments based on what linguistic phenomena are present in the elicitation material and what kinds of supporting contexts accompany the sentences. In this story, she describes each member of nɬeʔkepmxcín lab primarily based on these two factors while incorporating other characteristics she knows about each lab member.

form: 4 Readers who are curious about the identit ies of the people discussed in the story can email the authors for information.

This is a story. I’m going to talk about the work of these people who work on the other people’s language. The first one there, she is a woman. She has a child. He is a man. That man left. He went to a different land. He followed what he wanted to do. His mother comes from a different land. She also has a dog. She really loves him. She must have worked on a different people’s language for a long time. She writes to someone and sees what it’s like. There is one man who also works on the people’s language. He is a man. He comes from the USA. That man, he is always talking about legends and stories. He’s always asking what people are doing when they are trout fishing or net fishing.

form: There is one woman who works on the people’s language. She also comes from a different land. That land is very cold in the winter. There is a lot of snow and ice. Maybe her family is there. form: There is another woman with red hair. She comes from a different land. It is really far from this land. She is always smiling. Her earrings are always different. She also has a dog. Sometimes her dog jumps on her when she’s sitting and talking to me while we’re working.

form: One man, he’s very tall. He seems to have curly hair. He also has a dog. The dog wants to play when we are working. He asks me if I hear it. He asks me what this is and what that is, where this way is and where that way is.
gloss: the literal English translation of the story, §1, set as paragraphs. Its sentences are the translation lines of §5

form: One man, he really loves his dog. I’ve been told that he has just got ten married, but I’m not sure about that. He was hurt, but now it seems he’s healed. He’s always asking me about a branch. He almost manages to cut it but doesn’t. He always seems to be working on a fence. One woman, she always asks me about one word at a time. She says to me, “How do you pronounce this?” What she asks me is a lot sometimes. She changes her glasses and how her hair is. Sometimes I don’t recognize her.

form: One man, he has a dog too. He jumps on him when we ’re working. He has long hair. He is a good-natured man. He is always funny and smiling. He asks me if a man is able to make a drying rack. And tells me that he almost shot a deer but didn’t because the deer laid down. There is one woman that works on our language. She seems to always be happy. She asks me sometimes if I’m well. She told me she’s going to look for a job because she finished school. She asked me in the beginning if someone was able to kick something and if they managed to kick it. She walks while we work.
